title: Enforce TS coverage threshold in pre-commit (pnpm check), not just CI
description:
GAP: The hdf-converters TS branch-coverage threshold (90%, enforced by vitest --coverage config) only runs in CI's Coverage job. The pre-commit hook runs 'pnpm check', which calls 'pnpm test' (vitest run, no coverage), NOT 'pnpm test:coverage'. So a commit that drops branch coverage below 90% passes the local gate and only fails after push (happened on the ckl-converter PR: global TS branch coverage dipped to 89.5% from new under-covered files; CI Coverage job failed).

FIX OPTIONS:
1. Add a coverage step to the 'pnpm check' chain (root package.json) so the threshold is enforced before commit. Simplest, but lengthens EVERY commit's pre-commit hook by the cost of a coverage run (~tens of seconds for hdf-converters). That's a real tradeoff on commit latency.
2. Make it a lighter-weight check: only run coverage for packages with changed files, or run coverage but only fail on the global threshold (skip per-file noise).
3. Leave pre-commit as-is and instead document that contributors should run 'pnpm test:coverage' before pushing, plus keep the CI gate as the backstop. (Lowest effort, lowest friction, but doesn't actually close the gap.)
4. Move the threshold enforcement earlier via a fast incremental coverage tool.

Decision needed: is the added pre-commit latency worth catching coverage regressions locally vs. relying on the CI backstop? Lean on team's tolerance for hook duration (the hook already runs build+lint+typecheck+test+security and is not fast).

Scope: root package.json 'check'/'test' scripts and possibly per-package coverage scripts; the vitest coverage threshold config already exists. Surfaced during the ckl-converter PR (bidirectional CKL/CKLB).

title: hdf convert: handle already-HDF input gracefully + drop stale 'hdf-v2' naming
description:
Two related issues surfaced while spot-testing the CKL export path.

SYMPTOM: Running 'hdf convert <an-hdf-file>' with no --to auto-detects the input and dies confusingly:
  $ ./hdf convert /tmp/nessus-to-hdf.hdf
  Detected: HDF v2 (confidence: 80%)
  Error: no converter found for: hdf-v2-passthrough -> hdf
  Unrecognized source format: 'hdf-v2-passthrough'
  <dumps the full list of source formats>
The convert command detected source id 'hdf-v2-passthrough', defaulted the target to 'hdf', and looked up GetConverter('hdf-v2-passthrough','hdf') which doesn't exist.

FIX 1 (UX): When the input is already an HDF document and no --to is given, the CLI should NOT attempt an hdf->hdf conversion and dump the registry. It should either (a) print a clear message like 'input is already HDF; specify --to <format> to export (e.g. ckl, cklb, csv, xccdf, oscal-sar)', or (b) treat no-op/passthrough sensibly. Decide the right behavior in convert.go routing (hdf-cli/cmd/hdf/cmd/convert.go) where the detected source id + default dest are resolved.

FIX 2 (NAMING): The detection layer has bubbled up a stale 'hdf-v2' reference. The project convention is to call the format just 'hdf' with NO major-version suffix on function/field names (we are already on schema v3). The fingerprint ID 'hdf-v2-passthrough' and label 'HDF v2' are inconsistent with that. Reconcile:
  - hdf-converters/converters/hdf-v2-passthrough/go/fingerprint.go (ID 'hdf-v2-passthrough', Label 'HDF v2')
  - hdf-converters/converters/hdf-v2-passthrough/typescript/fingerprint.ts (+ fingerprint.test.ts)
  - registry/all/all.go import + any detection-test expectations (registry/all/all_test.go has a fixtureTests entry mapping hdf-to-xml/minimal.json -> 'hdf-v2-passthrough')
Consider whether the converter directory + fingerprint id should be renamed (e.g. 'hdf-passthrough' / label 'HDF') and what migration that implies for detection IDs consumers may key on. At minimum the user-facing label 'HDF v2' should not claim v2 when the current schema is v3.

Out of scope: the legacyhdf-to-hdf converter (that one legitimately ingests v1 InSpec exec-json and the v1/v2 distinction is real there). This is specifically about the hdf-v2-passthrough native-HDF detector + the convert UX.

Found during the ckl-converter PR (CKL/CKLB bidirectional support). Not blocking that PR.
notes: Fixed both issues. FIX 1 (convert.go): native-HDF input is detected as the passthrough id; runConvert now normalizes it to source 'hdf' so hdf->export converters resolve, and when no --to is given returns buildAlreadyHDFError() listing real export targets instead of an hdf->hdf no-op / registry dump. FIX 2 (rename): hdf-v2-passthrough -> hdf-passthrough, label 'HDF v2' -> 'HDF', exported FingerprintID const. Updated go/ts fingerprints + tests, registry/all import + detection test, register-all.ts, integration.test.ts. New CLI tests in convert_test.go.

title: Add ckl-to-hdf converter for parity with heimdall2/SAF CLI
description:
Heimdall2 / SAF CLI ship a CKL ingest converter (saf convert ckl2hdf). This repo currently has no equivalent. CKL is the DISA STIG Viewer manual-checklist XML format — used when STIG rules don't have OVAL automation and an assessor records pass/fail by hand. Distinct from XCCDF: XCCDF is the rule/check format (and can wrap both OVAL and OCIL); CKL is the manual-fill workflow output of the STIG Viewer GUI.

Format reference: https://public.cyber.mil/stigs/srg-stig-tools/ — STIG Viewer

The converter should:
- Ingest .ckl XML (and the newer .cklb JSON variant DISA introduced for STIG Viewer 3.x — research whether parity with heimdall2 includes cklb)
- Produce an HDF results document (EvaluatedRequirement per <VULN>)
- Map STATUS values (Open / NotAFinding / Not_Reviewed / Not_Applicable) to HDF Result_Status
- Pull NIST/CCI/severity tags from <STIG_DATA> entries
- For v3.2: set verificationMethod=manual-by-design (CKL is by-design a manual workflow — that's the whole reason it exists)
- For v3.2: derive controlType from NIST family prefix per the helper, since CKL files carry NIST tags via CCIs

title: [epic] HDF v3.2.0: control classification fields on Requirement_Core
description:
Add three optional, backward-compatible enum fields to Requirement_Core
to make catalogs self-describing about classification, verification
intent, and within-baseline applicability. Each axis is rooted in
distinctions the frameworks themselves already make; HDF currently
forces consumers to lose the information or carry parallel annotations
outside HDF.

Fields:

  - controlType: policy | procedure | technical | management | operational
    NIST 800-53 / SP 800-53A explicitly distinguishes these categories.
    Whether a control is policy vs. procedure vs. technical determines
    whether it's authored, deployed, or attested — different artifacts,
    different verification workflows. Translation across frameworks
    (NIST -> CIS -> CMMC) cannot preserve fidelity without it. Today
    consumers derive heuristically from family conventions, often
    inconsistently.

  - verificationMethod: automated | manual-by-design |
                        manual-pending-automation | hybrid
    The current "code: null" overloads two distinct cases: inherently
    manual (FedRAMP 20x KSIs are statement-form by design) vs.
    automation-could-exist-but-doesn't-yet (a STIG rule missing <fix>).
    Automation-coverage metrics across frameworks cannot be computed
    from HDF alone today.

  - applicability: required | optional | advisory
    Frameworks already carry this in incompatible forms: FedRAMP rev5
    OSCAL CORE prop, FedRAMP 20x FRMR inline 'Optional:' markdown,
    CIS Implementation Group membership, CMMC sublevels. No uniform
    HDF expression exists. Distinct from severity (risk weight) and
    status (lifecycle state). Programs needing richer semantics can
    layer them onto props[] / tags{}.

All three fields are optional. Existing v3.1.x documents validate
cleanly under v3.2.0. Existing consumers (Heimdall, hdf-converters,
hdf-validators) continue to work unchanged; surfacing the new fields
is opt-in.

Why these three axes: each describes a different axis (kind of control,
how it's verified, whether mandatory). Together they fully describe a
requirement's shape in a baseline, making HDF self-sufficient as a
wire format for any framework that already carries these distinctions.
N x M consumer-framework integrations collapse to N + M.

Out of scope:
  - controlFamily field (derive from id prefix)
  - requiredEvidenceTypes (premature, revisit if pull develops)
  - Inheritance/Override doc clarification (separate effort)

Note: replaces orphaned ghost bead hdf-libs-wcg3 (br lookup index
inconsistent for that ID; recreated here to update enum to 5 values).

title: Add sigstore provenance attestation to publish workflow
description:
Add sigstore provenance attestation to the publish workflow. Two-line change once the workflow exists: `id-token: write` permission on the release job, and `NPM_CONFIG_PROVENANCE: "true"` env var (or `--provenance` flag on the publish command).

Together these instruct npm CLI to generate a sigstore attestation tying each published tarball cryptographically to the GitHub Actions run that built it. Consumers can verify via `npm view <pkg> --json | jq .attestations`.

Why this matters: the chokidar 4.0.1 → 4.0.2 attestation gap caused months of downstream pain (npm/cli#8018, paulmillr/chokidar#1440). Once a package has shipped with provenance, consumers' supply-chain tooling expects it; losing it later requires per-package trust exceptions across the ecosystem.

Reference: docs/plans/2026-04-25-publishing-pipeline.md §"Step 6 (provenance bullets)"

Depends on Card C (workflow must exist to add the permission to).

Acceptance criteria:
- [ ] `id-token: write` permission present on the release job in .github/workflows/release.yml
- [ ] `NPM_CONFIG_PROVENANCE: "true"` env var (or `--provenance` flag) on publish step
- [ ] First post-merge publish produces a verifiable attestation (verified via `npm view <pkg> --json | jq .attestations` after Will provisions NPM_TOKEN)
- [ ] No regression on prior cards' acceptance criteria

title: SBOM-to-System workflow: import CycloneDX/SPDX inventory into System components
description:
When a CycloneDX or SPDX file contains no vulnerabilities (pure SBOM inventory), it should populate an HDF System document rather than produce an empty Results document.

Workflow:
- hdf system create --from sbom.cdx.json --component-name WebTier → new System with component
- hdf system add-component --system system.json --from sbom.cdx.json --component-name AuthService → add component to existing System  
- hdf system update-component --system system.json --component-name WebTier --from sbom-new.cdx.json → update component's sbomRef and metadata

Extract from SBOM: component name, version, type, supplier from metadata.component. Store sbomRef (URI to original file) and sbomFormat on the System component.

The CycloneDX converter should detect SBOM-only input (no vulnerabilities) and return an error directing users to the system workflow instead of producing invalid Results.

Aligns with NIST OSCAL CSWP 53 direction for SBOM integration (link-based, not inlined). Our System schema already has sbomRef and sbomFormat fields on components.

Security audit tightened to block on moderate+ vulns.

title: Unified xccdf-to-hdf converter with auto-detection and benchmark→baseline support
description:
Refactor the existing xccdf-results-to-hdf converter into a unified xccdf-to-hdf converter that:

1. Auto-detects whether input is a benchmark (no TestResult elements) or results (has TestResult elements)
2. Routes to the appropriate conversion path:
   - Benchmark → HDF Baseline (NEW — extracts requirements, tags, descriptions from XCCDF Groups/Rules)
   - Results → HDF Results (existing logic from xccdf-results-to-hdf)
3. Supports three CLI source format names:
   - 'xccdf' — auto-detect input type, produce appropriate HDF output
   - 'xccdf-benchmark' — require benchmark input, error if TestResult elements found
   - 'xccdf-results' — require results input, error if no TestResult elements found
4. Must handle both XCCDF 1.1 and 1.2 namespaces (ties into bx2)
5. Not DISA-specific — must work with any valid XCCDF benchmark (CIS, OpenSCAP, etc.)

Detection logic: parse XML, check for TestResult elements (namespace-aware). Present/absent determines routing.

This replaces the need for an ad-hoc script to produce HDF Baseline fixtures from XCCDF benchmarks — the converter itself becomes the canonical tool for that.
notes: ARF (Assessment Results Format) files embed XCCDF results inside them. The existing xccdf-results-to-hdf converter already handles ARF via the 'arf' source alias. The unified converter must preserve this: 'arf' should remain a valid source format name that routes to the results path (ARF files always contain results, never bare benchmarks). Ensure the auto-detection logic also recognizes ARF wrapper elements and routes correctly when input is ARF rather than standalone XCCDF.

title: Fix double URL-encoding of project path in GitLab fetcher
description:
## Bug
When using `--project wdower/juice-shop` (namespace/path format), the GitLab fetcher returns 404. Numeric project IDs (`--project 1`) work fine.

## Root Cause
In `hdf-cli/internal/fetchers/gitlab.go`, line ~139-148: `url.PathEscape(f.params.ProjectID)` produces `wdower%2Fjuice-shop`, which is then assigned to `url.URL.Path`. When Go serializes the URL via `.String()`, it re-encodes the `%` to `%25`, producing `wdower%252Fjuice-shop` in the actual HTTP request. GitLab doesn't find that project ID, returns 404.

## Fix
Set both `url.URL.Path` (decoded) and `url.URL.RawPath` (pre-encoded) so Go preserves the intended encoding. Or construct the URL string directly without going through `url.URL`.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `hdf fetch gitlab --project wdower/juice-shop ...` works (namespace/path format)
- [ ] `hdf fetch gitlab --project 1 ...` still works (numeric ID)
- [ ] Test added for namespace/path project IDs with slashes
- [ ] Existing fetcher tests still pass
close_reason: Fixed: URL double-encoding (RawPath), cross-platform glab config (adrg/xdg), hostname-with-port matching. Commit 90996ed.

title: Add --ca-cert and --insecure TLS flags to all API-based fetchers
description:
## Problem
None of our API-based fetchers (Splunk, SonarQube, GitLab, AWS Config) support custom CA certificates or insecure TLS bypass. SAF CLI didn't have this either. Users with internal instances behind self-signed or corporate CA certs cannot use live fetch mode.

## Requirements (12-factor CLI best practices)
1. **--ca-cert <path>** flag: Load a PEM CA bundle for custom certificate authorities (corporate PKI, mkcert, internal CAs)
2. **--insecure** flag: Skip TLS verification entirely (dev/test only, with a visible warning printed to stderr)
3. **Environment variable fallback**: Support HDF_CA_CERT and HDF_INSECURE env vars (12-factor: store config in the environment)
4. Implement once in shared fetcher infrastructure, not per-fetcher
5. AWS Config fetcher: wire through aws-sdk-go-v2 custom HTTP client

## Design Notes
- Go: Build a shared `NewHTTPClient(caCertPath string, insecure bool)` in `hdf-cli/internal/fetchers/shared.go` that returns a configured \*http.Client
- All fetchers call this instead of `&http.Client{}`
- --insecure should print a warning to stderr: 'WARNING: TLS certificate verification is disabled. This is insecure.'
- Cobra flags registered at the parent 'convert' command level so they apply to all fetchers
- TypeScript: Not needed immediately (CLI is Go-only), but if we add a TS fetcher layer later, use a custom https.Agent with `rejectUnauthorized: false` or `ca: [pemBuffer]`

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `hdf convert splunk to hdf --live --ca-cert /path/to/ca.pem ...` works with custom CA
- [ ] `hdf convert gitlab to hdf --live --insecure ...` works with self-signed certs (prints warning)
- [ ] HDF_CA_CERT=/path/to/ca.pem hdf convert sonarqube to hdf --live ... works
- [ ] All fetcher tests still pass (no regression)
- [ ] --insecure prints visible warning to stderr
notes: [2026-03-03] Security review finding MED-4 confirms this need. Also fold in MED-2 (default to HTTPS-only, require --allow-insecure-http for plain HTTP fetcher connections to prevent token exposure).
close_reason: Implemented: --ca-cert and --insecure flags on all fetchers with shared TLS infrastructure, env var fallback, 11 tests

title: Add ARF (Asset Reporting Format) support to XCCDF converter
description:
ARF (NIST IR 7694) is an XML wrapper format that packages one or more XCCDF TestResults along with asset metadata (IP, hostname, FQDN) and relationships. OpenSCAP and other SCAP scanners produce ARF as their primary output format.

The XCCDF converter should be extended to:
1. Detect whether input is raw XCCDF or ARF-wrapped XCCDF (root element is arf:asset-report-collection vs xccdf:Benchmark/TestResult)
2. If ARF: extract all arf:report elements containing xccdf:TestResult, extract asset metadata from arf:assets, and delegate each TestResult to existing XCCDF conversion logic
3. Produce a multi-baseline HDF output when multiple TestResults exist (one baseline per report)
4. Enrich HDF targets with ARF asset identification (IP addresses, MAC addresses, FQDN, hostname)
5. Register 'arf' as a CLI alias for the xccdf converter (similar to inspec-to-hdf aliasing legacyhdf)

Key ARF structure:
- Root: arf:asset-report-collection
- arf:report-requests — embeds or references the benchmark used
- arf:assets — computing-device with IP/MAC/FQDN/hostname
- arf:reports — contains one or more arf:report, each wrapping an xccdf:TestResult
- core:relationships — links reports to assets via arfvocab:isAbout

Schema: https://csrc.nist.gov/schema/asset-reporting-format/1.1/asset-reporting-format_1.1.0.xsd
Spec: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/IR/nistir7694.pdf

The new findXmlValues utility from hdf-utilities is well-suited for traversing ARF's nested structure to locate TestResult elements and asset metadata.
close_reason: ARF support implemented in both Go and TypeScript converters, with format detection, CLI alias, and comprehensive tests. All 37 Go converter tests pass (28 XCCDF + 9 ARF), all 61 TypeScript tests pass (48 XCCDF + 13 ARF), all format detection tests pass, and CLI tests pass.

title: Implement format detection and routing in tool converters
description:
Tool converters (e.g. gosec-to-hdf) should detect the input format and delegate to shared format converters when appropriate.

## Design
Each tool converter's Convert function:
1. Runs format fingerprinting on input bytes (is it SARIF? JUnit XML? CycloneDX? native?)
2. If shared format → delegates to the shared format converter (e.g. sarif-to-hdf)
3. If native → uses tool-specific parsing
4. Optionally applies tool-specific enrichment after shared conversion

## Fingerprinting Heuristics
- SARIF: JSON with $schema containing "sarif" OR top-level version (string) + runs (array)
- JUnit XML: XML with <testsuites> or <testsuite> root element
- CycloneDX: JSON with bomFormat field OR XML with CycloneDX namespace
- XCCDF: XML with XCCDF namespace
- Native: tool-specific detection (e.g. gosec has GosecVersion + Issues fields)

## Shared format converter location
hdf-converters/formats/{sarif,junit,cyclonedx,xccdf}/{go,typescript}/

## Affected tool converters (SARIF-capable)
gosec, snyk, zap, jfrog-xray, fortify, veracode + any future tool that supports SARIF export

## Dependencies
- Requires enriched SARIF converter (comprehensive rules/relationships/suppressions/taxonomy parsing)
- Existing tool-specific converters continue working for native format input

---

## Progress
- [x] Format detection utility (Go + TypeScript) in shared/go/formatdetect.go, shared/typescript/formatdetect.ts
- [x] gosec converter routes SARIF input to shared SARIF converter (Go + TypeScript)
- [x] Tests: format detection unit tests (13 Go, 11 TS), gosec SARIF routing integration tests
- [ ] Other SARIF-capable tool converters (snyk, zap, jfrog-xray, etc.) — pending those converters being built
close_reason: Format detection utility and gosec SARIF routing complete. Remaining SARIF-capable tools will integrate format detection as part of their individual converter beads.

- Pointer helpers: sarif defines stringPtr/floatPtr, sonarqube defines stringPtr, aws-config defines ptr[T any] — should be one generic Ptr[T]()
- HTML tag stripping: nessus and sonarqube each define their own regex-based strip function
- RFC3339 multi-format timestamp parsing: aws-config, nessus, sonarqube each implement their own fallback parse loop
All four patterns are small enough to land in a single shared file with tests.

title: Audit converters for format-level commonality
description:
## Architecture Decision: Format-Level Routing

### Problem
Many security tools output multiple formats (native JSON, SARIF, SonarQube Generic, etc.). Users shouldn't need to know which converter to use — `hdf convert gosec to hdf` should work regardless of whether the input is gosec native JSON or gosec SARIF output.

### Decision: Strategy B — Rich shared format converters + tool-level format detection

Tool converters (e.g. gosec-to-hdf) become thin routing layers:
1. Detect what format the input is in (native JSON? SARIF? JUnit XML?)
2. If shared format → delegate to shared format converter
3. If native → use tool-specific parsing
4. Optionally apply tool-specific enrichment after shared conversion

### Shared Format Converters Needed
- **SARIF** (covers: gosec, snyk, zap, jfrog-xray, semgrep, CodeQL, trivy, checkov, ESLint, fortify, veracode)
- **JUnit XML** (covers: test frameworks, CI/CD outputs)
- **CycloneDX** (covers: SBOM tools — trivy, syft, snyk, cdxgen)
- **XCCDF** (covers: OpenSCAP, DISA STIGs)

### SARIF Converter Gaps (current → needed)
Current converter is minimal. Must add:
- `rules[]` definitions (name, description, helpUri)
- `rules[].relationships` → CWE taxonomy extraction
- `tool.driver.supportedTaxonomies` → CWE/OWASP awareness
- `result.suppressions[]` → notReviewed status with justification
- `rules[].properties` → confidence, tags, custom metadata
- `rules[].defaultConfiguration.level` → severity when result.level is absent
- Proper severity granularity from rule metadata

### Impact on Converter Count
- ~14 proprietary-only tools still need dedicated converters
- ~5-8 SARIF-capable tools can delegate to enriched SARIF converter
- 3 standard formats (JUnit, CycloneDX, XCCDF) get dedicated shared converters
- Net: fewer converters to build and maintain

### Format Detection
Use fingerprinting (check for `$schema`+`version`+`runs` for SARIF, `<testsuites>` for JUnit, `bomFormat` for CycloneDX, etc.) rather than requiring the user to specify format.

---
## Progress
- [x] SARIF converter enriched with full spec support (2026-02-21): rules[], relationships, taxonomies, suppressions, kind mapping, fixes, codeFlows, snippets, fingerprints, level fallback chain
- [ ] JUnit XML shared format converter
- [ ] CycloneDX shared format converter
- [ ] XCCDF shared format converter
close_reason: SARIF converter enriched with full 2.1.0 spec support. Remaining shared format converters (JUnit, CycloneDX, XCCDF) will be built as standalone tasks before individual tool converters.

title: Add junit-to-hdf converter
description: Implement a converter from JUnit XML test result format to HDF. JUnit XML is widely produced by test frameworks (pytest, Jest, Maven Surefire, etc.). Should include both Go and TypeScript implementations, CLI integration, and >90% test coverage per project standards.

title: Add inspec-to-hdf converter
description:
InSpec JSON output needs a dedicated converter for HDF v2. In v1, HDF was structurally derived from InSpec output format, so no converter was needed. In v2, a converter is required.

InSpec JSON output format: { platform: {...}, profiles: [ { name, version, title, controls: [ { id, title, desc, impact, refs, tags, results: [...] } ] } ] }

This format is the same as the legacyhdf-to-hdf converter input. The inspec-to-hdf converter should:
- Be a thin, well-named wrapper that clearly targets current InSpec output (v4/v5+)
- Set dataSource.name = 'Chef InSpec' and dataSource.version from the InSpec version field in output
- Handle multi-profile InSpec runs (one baseline per profile, or merged - TBD)
- Handle wrapper profiles (InSpec profiles that depend on other profiles)
- May share parsing logic with legacyhdf-to-hdf or may replace it once legacy migration is complete

Design question: should this share code with legacyhdf-to-hdf or be independent? The legacyhdf converter handles HDF v1 data that was already processed by Heimdall, which may differ slightly from raw InSpec output.
close_reason: Resolved via alias: InSpec exec-json is identical to HDF v1.0, so legacyhdf-to-hdf handles it. Added CLI alias (hdf convert inspec to hdf) in b1a1d8d and ubi9 STIG fixture in 686c001.

title: HDF schema: separate data-source from tool-creator in Generator
description:
The current Generator field conflates two distinct concepts: (1) the source tool that produced the original scan data (e.g. Nessus, gosec, SonarQube) and (2) the software that actually created the HDF file (e.g. hdf-converters, hdf-cli). Both need to be representable independently so consumers can determine provenance without inspecting converter internals.

Proposed change: split Generator into two fields or sub-fields:
- source (or dataSource): name/version of the original scanning tool
- converter (or creator): name/version of the HDF-producing tool

This is a schema-level change (hdf-schema) with downstream impact on:
- hdf-schema: TypeScript type definitions and JSON schema
- hdf-schema Go package: struct definitions
- hdf-validators: update validation rules for new/renamed fields
- hdf-converters (all converters, both Go and TypeScript): update Generator construction
- hdf-cli: update CLI version injection
- hdf-parsers: update any field references
- Possibly hdf-to-csv, hdf-to-xml output-side converters

Design questions to resolve before implementation:
- New top-level fields vs nested under existing Generator?
- Backwards compatibility: is the old Generator field deprecated or removed?
- Field names: source/converter, dataSource/creator, or something else?
- Version field: does each sub-field carry its own version, or shared?
- How should converters that have no meaningful 'source version' (e.g. static file import) populate the source field?
close_reason: Implemented as dataSource field on HdfResults (schema + all converters) in commits 7c2f694 and 1a4a878.

title: Implement SonarQube live fetch mode
description:
Add live API fetch mode to the SonarQube converter so users can run a single command instead of manually capturing the /api/issues/search response.

## What
hdf convert sonarqube to hdf --live --url https://sq.example.com --token TOKEN --project my-proj output.json

The fetcher lives in hdf-cli/internal/fetchers/sonarqube.go. It calls the SonarQube REST API (no extra Go deps — standard net/http), paginates /api/issues/search, and marshals the combined response into the same IssuesResponse format the file-based converter already reads. File-based mode continues to work unchanged.

## API mocking
Tests must not require a live SonarQube server. Use httptest.Server serving canned JSON responses pointed at via --url flag. Coordinate with hdf-libs-6b0.21.2 (Improve SonarQube testing without live server).

## Credentials / flags
--url (required), --token (required), --project (required), --branch (optional), --org (optional), --insecure (skip TLS verify)
close_reason: Implemented in hdf-cli/internal/fetchers/sonarqube.go + fetch_sonarqube.go. Token via SONARQUBE_TOKEN env var (not --token flag). Pagination via ps=500, capped at 10k pages. httptest-based tests, no live server required.

title: hdf-cli: improve test coverage for stats and query gaps
description:
Mutation testing (Gremlins) identified two clusters of uncovered mutations in hdf-cli.

## Gap 1: stats.go — status counters (10 uncovered mutations, lines 84–90 and 174–180)
The `++` counter increments for `StatusError`, `StatusNotReviewed`, and `StatusSkipped` in both the global stats accumulator and the per-baseline breakdown are never exercised. Tests only create controls with `passed`/`failed`/`not_applicable` status.

**Fix**: Add test cases in `stats_test.go` that include controls with `error`, `not_reviewed`, and `skipped` result statuses and assert the counter values are non-zero.

## Gap 2: query.go — compareImpact operators (7 uncovered mutations, lines 329–333)
The `compareImpact` function has a switch over `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`, `=` but tests only cover the equality case via `--impact` flag. The boundary comparison branches (`>0.5`, `>=0.7`, `<0.4`, `<=0.3`) are not tested.

**Fix**: Add `query_test.go` cases using each impact operator (`>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`) and verify correct filtering.

## Other minor gaps
- `convert.go:87-89`: The error message branch for "both source and dest formats unrecognized" — add a test that uses two completely unknown format names and checks the error message contains the expected suggestion text.
- `list.go:177`: `truncateTitle` length edge case — test a title exactly at the max length boundary.

## Stryker config
`hdf-utilities/stryker.config.cjs` is in place for re-running. Use `gremlins unleash --timeout-coefficient 20` for Go.

## Resolution
Added to `stats_test.go`: `TestCalculateStats_AllStatuses` (unit, all 6 statuses via EffectiveStatus), `TestStatsCommand_AllStatuses_JSON` (integration, schema-valid result statuses covering notApplicable/notReviewed/error branches). Added to `query_test.go`: `TestQueryCommand_TextOutput_ImpactFilter` (exercises >, >=, < operators and the fmt.Printf text path), `TestQueryCommand_TextOutput_TitleTruncation` (56+ char title → `title[:52]+"..."`). Added to `convert_test.go`: `TestConvertCommand_ErrorMessages` (covers all 3 branches of `buildConverterNotFoundError`).

title: hdf-validators: update import assertions to 'with' syntax
description:
The `typescript/index.ts` file uses deprecated `assert { type: 'json' }` import attribute syntax (lines 5–12) for JSON schema imports. This should be updated to the modern `with { type: 'json' }` syntax.

## Why
- `assert` is deprecated in the ECMAScript spec; `with` is the current standard
- Stryker 9.x's Babel-based instrumenter cannot parse `assert { type: 'json' }` — this blocks mutation testing on hdf-validators entirely
- Updating unblocks Stryker and aligns with the current standard

## Changes Required
- `hdf-validators/typescript/index.ts`: change all `assert { type: 'json' }` → `with { type: 'json' }` on JSON schema imports
- Verify `pnpm test` still passes after the change
- Re-run `npx stryker run` with `hdf-validators/stryker.config.cjs` to confirm Stryker can now instrument the file

## Related
- Stryker config already exists at `hdf-validators/stryker.config.cjs`

## Resolution
All 9 `assert { type: 'json' }` import attributes changed to `with { type: 'json' }` in `hdf-validators/typescript/index.ts`. Pure syntax change; no logic affected.

- DefectDojo provides gold standard with 17+ test fixtures covering edge cases

title: Address SonarQube 10,000 record limit
description:
Filter-based partitioning for projects with true >10,000 issues is not yet implemented.

What was done: fetcher caps pagination at maxPages=10,000 (ps=500 per page = up to 5M issues). For most real projects this is sufficient.

What remains: if a project hits the Elasticsearch 10k result limit on a single unfiltered query, the API will return at most 10,000 issues regardless of page count. To handle those projects, we need to split queries by severity/type/language/date range and merge results. This is the original scope of this issue.

Reference: https://community.sonarsource.com/t/how-to-retrieve-more-than-10-000-results-using-api-issues-search/153628
close_reason: Implemented severity-partitioned fetching: when project exceeds the Elasticsearch 10K result cap, fetcher automatically re-queries per severity level (BLOCKER, CRITICAL, MAJOR, MINOR, INFO), deduplicates by issue key, and merges results. Logs warnings for partitioning and per-severity counts. Warns if a single severity exceeds 10K.

title: Add bulk file operations to hdf-cli
description:
Enhance hdf-cli commands to process multiple files in a single invocation with summary reporting.

## Requirements

### Input Methods
- Multiple file arguments: `hdf validate file1.json file2.json file3.json`
- Glob patterns: `hdf validate scans/*.json` or `hdf validate "**/*-results.json"`

### Output Formats
- **Default**: Summary table showing per-file results
  ```
  Validating 10 files...
  ✓ scan-1.json         (results)
  ✓ scan-2.json         (results)
  ✗ scan-3.json         (results) - baselines[0].name: is required
  
  Results: 8/10 passed, 2 failed
  ```
- **--json**: JSON output for scripting/automation
- **--yaml**: YAML output as alternative structured format

### Error Handling
- Continue processing all files even if some fail
- Exit with non-zero code if ANY files fail
- Research and use correct GNU-style exit codes:
  - 0 = all files processed successfully
  - Non-zero = at least one file failed
  - Different codes for different failure types?

### Processing
- Sequential processing (not parallel)
- Progress indication for large batches

### Commands to Update
- `hdf validate` - validate multiple HDF files
- `hdf stats` - aggregate statistics across multiple files
- `hdf info` - show info for multiple files
- `hdf query` - query across multiple files
- `hdf list` - list requirements across multiple files
- ~~`hdf convert`~~ - skip (requires output file argument, complex)

## Implementation Notes

### File Expansion
- Need to handle glob patterns correctly
- Handle file not found errors gracefully
- Validate that globs match at least one file

### Exit Codes Research
Research proper GNU/POSIX exit codes:
- Standard: 0 = success, 1 = general error
- Consider: Different codes for validation vs I/O errors?
- Look at tools like: grep, find, ls for precedent

### Output Format Consistency
- All bulk operations should use similar output structure
- --json format should be consistent across commands
- --yaml should mirror JSON structure

### Testing
- Test with large numbers of files (100+)
- Test with glob patterns that match nothing
- Test with mix of valid and invalid files
- Test with --json and --yaml output parsing

## Examples

```bash
# Validate multiple files
hdf validate scan1.json scan2.json scan3.json

# Validate with glob
hdf validate scans/*.json

# JSON output for CI/CD
hdf validate "**/*.json" --json > results.json

# Stats across multiple files
hdf stats scan-*.json

# Query across files
hdf query "baselines[0].name" results/*.json
```

## Success Criteria
- Multiple file arguments work for all commands
- Glob patterns expand correctly
- Summary table is clear and useful
- --json output is valid and parseable
- Exit codes follow GNU conventions
- All existing single-file functionality preserved
- Tests cover bulk operations
close_reason: Bulk file ops for validate/list/query/convert. -k flag, glob expansion, clean error output, verb-specific summaries.

title: Review converter output for unnecessary null fields
description:
SYSTEMATIC REFACTOR: Nullable vs Optional Fields in HDF Schema

## Problem Statement
The HDF schema currently uses nullable patterns ("type": ["string", "null"]) for 123 fields across all schemas. This was originally intended to make fields optional, but in JSON Schema, nullable means "required to be present, but can have null value." This causes:
- Verbose output with explicit null values for unused fields
- Confusion about semantic intent
- Incompatibility with Go omitempty tags
- Wasted bytes in serialized JSON

## Current State
Total nullable fields: 123
- "type": ["type", "null"]" pattern: 96 fields
- "anyOf": [{$ref or type}, {"type": "null"}]" pattern: 27 fields

Distribution:
- common.schema.json: ~40 fields
- target.schema.json: ~50 fields
- result.schema.json: ~5 fields (runTime, resource, resourceId, message, exception, backtrace, status)
- hdf-results.schema.json: ~5 fields (depends, parentBaseline, description, inspecVersion, statusMessage)
- hdf-baseline.schema.json: ~2 fields (depends, remediation)
- extensions.schema.json: ~6 fields
- statistics.schema.json: ~7 fields
- platform.schema.json: ~1 field

## Observed Issues
From compliance.nessus conversion:
1. depends: null (1 occurrence at baseline level)
2. backtrace: null (5 occurrences at result level)

These should be omitted entirely when not provided.

## Root Cause
Schema design misunderstanding: nullable ≠ optional in JSON Schema.

For optional fields that can be omitted:
- DON'T: "type": ["string", "null"] with field not in required array
- DO: "type": "string" with field not in required array

The nullable pattern makes serializers include "field": null in output.

## Systematic Audit Plan

### Phase 1: Categorize All 123 Nullable Fields
For each field, determine:
1. Truly nullable (semantic difference between absent and null)
   - Example: status field where null = "not determined" vs absent = "not applicable"
2. Should be optional (no semantic difference, just omit when not present)
   - Metadata: title, description, version
   - Result details: backtrace, resource, resourceId, exception, message
   - Baseline metadata: depends, parentBaseline, statusMessage
3. Required with defaults (converters should always populate)

### Phase 2: Update Schemas (TDD Approach)
For each field categorized as "should be optional":
1. Update tests first to expect omission (not null)
2. Change schema:
   - "type": ["primitive", "null"] → "type": "primitive"
   - "anyOf": [{...}, {"type": "null"}] → {...}
3. Regenerate types from schema
4. Update helpers/converters to conditionally include fields
5. Verify tests pass

### Phase 3: Update Converters
For each converter (sarif-to-hdf, nessus-to-hdf, etc.):
- TypeScript: Conditional object construction (only add fields when present)
- Go: Verify omitempty tags work correctly after regeneration
- Update tests to verify omission behavior

### Phase 4: Documentation
- Document nullable vs optional distinction in schema README
- Add examples of when to use each pattern
- Update converter development guide

## Files to Audit
- hdf-schema/src/schemas/primitives/common.schema.json
- hdf-schema/src/schemas/primitives/target.schema.json
- hdf-schema/src/schemas/primitives/result.schema.json
- hdf-schema/src/schemas/primitives/extensions.schema.json
- hdf-schema/src/schemas/primitives/statistics.schema.json
- hdf-schema/src/schemas/primitives/platform.schema.json
- hdf-schema/src/schemas/hdf-results.schema.json
- hdf-schema/src/schemas/hdf-baseline.schema.json

## Expected Outcome
- Cleaner JSON output with no unnecessary null fields
- Clear semantic distinction between truly nullable and optional fields
- Better Go omitempty compatibility
- Smaller serialized JSON files
- Clearer schema intent for developers

## Priority
Medium - Not critical for functionality, but impacts:
- Data quality and readability
- Schema clarity and maintainability
- Output file size
- Developer experience

## Notes
- Start with depends and backtrace as proof-of-concept
- Most fields will likely become truly optional
- Few (if any) fields have true semantic need for null vs absent distinction

title: Library 5: hdf-extension-graph
description:
Client-side graph processing library for InSpec profile extension/overlay patterns. Builds bidirectional extension graphs from existing HDF schema fields (parentProfile, depends[], code, control id) without adding redundant computed fields to the schema.

Key capabilities:
- Build bidirectional graph from parentProfile links between baselines
- Link requirements by matching id across profiles
- Compute fullCode (concatenated from all layers), extensionChain, and modification detection on demand
- Provide ContextualizedBaseline and ContextualizedRequirement wrapper types
- Port Heimdall2's context.ts algorithm

Architectural decision: Keep schema minimal, do all graph processing client-side at load time. Follows database normalization principles and OSCAL precedent (profiles resolved at processing time). Performance target <200ms for 1000+ requirements.

Terminology: 'Extension' was chosen over 'overlay' — overlay is ambiguous (implies simple parent-child), while extension covers parent modification, wrapper bundling, and adding new controls.

Both had been bumped to 3.3.1 by the prior release, so leaving them at 3.3.1 while everything else moved to 3.3.2 would be exactly the lesson-#1 straggler drift the skill warns about. They were caught manually this release only because a post-sweep 'grep for remaining v<OLD> requires' check flagged them.

## Fix
Replace the hardcoded go.mod enumeration in Phase 2 with dynamic discovery, e.g.:
  grep -rl 'github.com/mitre/hdf-libs/[^ ]*/v3 v<OLD>' --include=go.mod . | grep -v node_modules
and bump every match. Keep the post-sweep verification grep ('no hdf-libs/.*/v3 v<OLD> require remains anywhere') as a hard gate. Also update the Quick-checklist line '5 go.mod files' to not assume a fixed count.

## Also worth fixing in the skill (smaller)
Phase 7 should remind to branch the release commit (release/vX-prep) rather than commit on main — this release the bump was first committed on main and had to be moved to a branch. The 'branch first on default branch' rule should be explicit in Phase 7.

title: hdf verify: validate an HDF artifact against its embedded source-provenance checksum
description:
Add an `hdf verify` command that checks an HDF document against the SHA-256 source-provenance hash embedded in it (baselines[].resultsChecksum / originalChecksum and root integrity) — NOT against the serialized output bytes.

## Behavior (proposed)
- `hdf verify <hdf-file> --input <source-file>`: recompute SHA-256 of the source file, compare to the artifact's embedded resultsChecksum/integrity. Exit 0 + message on match; non-zero + clear message on mismatch.
- `hdf verify <a.hdf> <b.hdf>`: compare the embedded source-provenance checksums of two HDF artifacts (the cross-implementation 'same source?' check) without needing the original input.
- `hdf verify <hdf-file>` (no other args): print the embedded checksum(s) for manual comparison.
- Implement in Go (CLI); consider a TS lib export so Heimdall/other JS consumers share the logic.

## Taxonomy / positioning
Sibling to the existing `hdf validate` (schema validity). validate = 'is this well-formed against the HDF schema'; verify = 'does this match its claimed source / is its provenance intact'. Both are document-level verbs, consistent with convert/query/diff. Distinct from the per-tool network-connectivity meaning of 'verify' that bead rtyy removes.
design:
Verify focuses on the SOURCE-input hash, not output bytes — deliberately. Tracing the hashing in this repo (2026-06-29): both resultsChecksum and root integrity are SHA-256 over the RAW INPUT bytes (the source tool output) via shared.InputChecksum/InputIntegrity (Go) and inputChecksum/inputIntegrity (TS). Nothing hashes the serialized HDF output and there is no output-signing path.

So the stable, meaningful identity of an HDF artifact is 'which source scan it derived from' — captured by the embedded checksum, independent of converter language, converter version, and JSON serialization. Two artifacts from the same source produced by different implementations (Go CLI vs TS Heimdall, or a future third-party HDF implementation in ANY language) carry the SAME source-provenance checksum even though their output bytes differ (key order, HTML escaping, omitempty, wall-clock fallbacks in ~7 converters, generator.version skew all make output bytes non-reproducible). Output byte-parity is therefore neither required (nothing consumes output bytes as a hash) nor achievable across implementations/versions. Verify must key on the source hash — the one thing every conformant HDF implementation can agree on. This is the robust answer to the 'CLI artifact vs Heimdall API artifact — same data?' use case: compare embedded resultsChecksum (matches), don't sha256 the files (won't).
notes: Conflict check vs existing 'verify' beads (done 2026-06-29): hdf-libs-rtyy currently owns 'hdf verify {splunk,tenable-sc}' = source-connectivity/credential check, and PLANS TO REMOVE that verify parent, migrating it to 'hdf fetch <tool> --check'. That FREES the verify verb for this document-level meaning — no behavior conflict. Coordinate sequencing: land this after (or reconcile with) rtyy so we don't reintroduce connectivity-verify semantics under the same verb. hdf-libs-pic0 (sigstore provenance attestation on the publish workflow) shares the provenance theme but a different object (npm tarballs, not HDF docs) — complementary. NOTE: a future 'deterministic/canonical output' initiative (remove wall-clock fallbacks + shared canonical serializer) would be needed only if we ever want byte-identical artifacts or to SIGN HDF documents — separate, lower priority, NOT a prerequisite for verify.

title: DRY: extract whole-second-UTC timestamp formatting in hdf-to-* export converters
description: The hdf-to-* export converters repeat '(...).toISOString().replace(/\.\d+Z$/, "Z")' to format timestamps to whole-second UTC for external formats: hdf-to-csaf-vex/typescript/converter.ts:179,249; hdf-to-cyclonedx-vex:246; hdf-to-openvex:82,109. title: legacyhdf converter drops valid v1 fields (refs, skip_message, etc.) — preserve in both Go+TS
description:
Discovered while fixing rf06 (Go/TS byte-parity). The legacyhdf-to-hdf converter (both languages, after rf06 converged TS to Go) DROPS several valid/meaningful v1 fields rather than mapping them to their v2 homes:

- results[].refs equivalent: control-level 'refs' (a valid Requirement_Core field) is dropped entirely. Go never mapped it; TS used to leak it (schema-invalidly) via passthrough, now also dropped.
- result skip_message: dropped. Should arguably map to result.message for skipped/notReviewed results (currently lost).
- v1 profile 'supports': Go never maps it (TS now omits empty; when non-empty it would diverge — untested). The flattened baseline also takes profile[0]'s metadata, dropping the leaf STIG profile's supports/attributes.
- component: only {type,name}+osName/osVersion(when target_id); v1 release without target_id is dropped.

rf06 intentionally converged TS->Go for byte-parity + schema-valid output (the passthroughs were emitting schema-INVALID fields). This bead tracks improving FIDELITY: map these valid v1 fields to their correct v2 homes in BOTH Go and TS (keeping parity), then regenerate snapshots. Lower priority than parity; no current test/consumer is blocked.
notes: Implementation complete + committed on branch fix/9q8o-legacyhdf-field-fidelity (commit 960084e), based on main 66257b1 (3.3.1). All 4 v1-field mappings done in Go+TS with parity: control refs->Requirement.refs (empty dropped); result skip_message->result.message (when no explicit message; ~35% of real results were losing it); profile supports->EvaluatedBaseline.supports (hyphenated->camelCase); platform release w/o target_id->component osName/osVersion. Coverage: Go 92.4%; TS 105 tests pass; refs+supports verified on real ubi9 fixture. three-layer-overlay snapshot regenerated via TS converter (minimal semantic diff: +40 message, +osName/osVersion). Orphaned snapshots (container/ubi9/wrapper) left untouched. Full pnpm check green. PENDING: user push + PR + merge to main, then close this bead. Ships as 3.3.2; legacy-HDF GH issue stays open until merged. Related follow-up: hdf-libs-81td (hdf verify command).
close_reason: Merged to main as 6d9bd4e (PR #120). All 4 v1-field mappings (refs, skip_message->message, supports, platform release) shipped in Go+TS with parity. Ships in 3.3.2 patch.

description:

title: Add BOM+NDJSON combined regression test once NDJSON + BOM fixes both land on main
description:
The NDJSON auto-detect fix (hdf-libs-86d2, PR #105, branch fix/trufflehog-ndjson-autodetect) and the BOM input fix (hdf-libs-7t7s, branch fix/bom-input-handling, commit 674ddb0) were developed on separate branches off main. Neither branch could test the BOM+NDJSON combination in isolation: the BOM branch is from main (no NDJSON fallback), and the NDJSON branch predates the BOM strip.

Once BOTH are merged to main, BOM-prefixed NDJSON should work end-to-end (readInputFile strips the BOM, then the registry first-line fallback fingerprints the NDJSON). Add a regression test to lock this in.

## Scope
- CLI e2e test in hdf-cli/cmd/hdf/cmd/converter_bom_test.go using writeBOMCopy on trufflehog-to-hdf/fixtures/input/ndjson-input.ndjson: convert with auto-detect (no --from) should detect TruffleHog and produce valid HDF.
- Optionally a registry unit test: DetectConverter on BOM-prefixed NDJSON resolves to the trufflehog fingerprint.

## Blocked on
Both PR #105 (NDJSON) and the BOM PR landing on main.

After rebasing the NDJSON branch onto main (which now has the BOM fix), added combined BOM+NDJSON regression tests: CLI e2e (TestBOM_NDJSON_AutoDetectConvert on ndjson-input.ndjson), Go registry unit, and TS registry unit. title: Add NDJSON handling guidance to /build-converter skill
description: The registry auto-detect NDJSON fix (hdf-libs-86d2, commit 5f7cadd) means auto-detect now succeeds on NDJSON input by fingerprinting the first line. But a converter only fully works on NDJSON if its Convert() also handles line-delimited input (whole-input array -> single object -> line-by-line fallback, as trufflehog-to-hdf does). A future converter author who writes only the array/single-object parse path would get a worse failure mode than before: auto-detect succeeds, then conversion fails. Add a checklist item / note to the /build-converter skill (.claude/commands/build-converter.md) telling authors to handle NDJSON in Convert() when the source tool can emit it, and to add an NDJSON fixture + test when so.

title: Bump vitepress to 2.x to clear vite GHSA-fx2h-pf6j-xcff
description:
Vite 5.4.21 (transitive under vitepress@1.6.4) carries GHSA-fx2h-pf6j-xcff (server.fs.deny bypass on Windows alternate paths). Patched in vite >=6.4.3, which requires a vitepress major bump.

title: Expose Security Hub filter flags on hdf fetch aws-securityhub
description:
The aws-securityhub fetcher Go library accepts an AwsSecurityFindingFilters via Params.Filters; the TS library accepts the same via FetchOptions.filters. The CLI doesn't expose these flags because constructing nested filter structs on a command line is awkward.

## Options to consider

1. **Specific common-case flags** — `--severity high,critical`, `--standard arn:...`, `--account-id 123456789012`. Maps to ProductFields, SeverityLabel, AwsAccountId filter slots. Covers ~80% of CLI use.
2. **JSON pass-through** — `--filter-json file.json` reads a literal JSON AwsSecurityFindingFilters and passes it to the SDK. Maximum expressiveness; ugly UX.
3. **Both** — common-case flags AS WELL AS --filter-json for advanced cases.

Recommend option 3 (both).

## Scope

- Add filter flags to `hdf fetch aws-securityhub`:
  - `--severity <label>[,<label>...]` (CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW/INFORMATIONAL)
  - `--workflow-status <status>[,<status>...]` (NEW/NOTIFIED/SUPPRESSED/RESOLVED)
  - `--filter-json <path>` (raw passthrough)
- Document in hdf-cli/README.md
- Unit tests covering each filter flag's translation to the SDK Input.Filters struct

## Dependencies

- Depends on hdf-libs-0seu (closed; the fetcher being filterable).

Priority P3 — the library can already be called with filters from heimdall2/saf-cli; CLI users wanting filters have a workaround (fetch all + jq).

title: Add hdf-to-asff converter to enable Security Hub BatchImportFindings push
description:
The aws-securityhub fetcher (commit f4f6c55) supports fetch + verify but NOT push. The bead spec (hdf-libs-0seu) called for pushHdfToSecurityHub via BatchImportFindings; that path requires an `hdf-to-asff` converter that translates HDF Results to ASFF findings before upload, which doesn't exist yet.

## Scope

- New converter at `hdf-converters/converters/hdf-to-asff/{go,typescript}/`.
- Reverse-mapping logic from heimdall2's `hdf-to-asff-mapper` if it exists; otherwise from ASFF format spec + the existing asff-to-hdf mappings.
- Round-trip parity tests with asff-to-hdf where possible.
- New `pushHdfToSecurityHub(client, hdf, opts)` exported by the aws-securityhub TS fetcher.
- New `PushHDF(ctx, hdf)` on AWSSecurityHubFetcher (Go).
- New `hdf push aws-securityhub` CLI command.

## Considerations

- ASFF requires a ProductArn pointing at your registered Security Hub product integration. Library must accept this as a caller parameter; surface a clear error if missing.
- BatchImportFindings has a 100-finding-per-call cap; reuse the Splunk push-chunking pattern.
- ASFF fields like CreatedAt, UpdatedAt, GeneratorId need defensible defaults — document the choices.

## Out of scope for this bead

- Cross-account / AssumeRole at push time (separate bead if needed).
- Filter-based deletion of previously-pushed findings (push-only here).

## Dependencies

- Depends on hdf-libs-0seu (closed; provides the fetcher infrastructure to extend).

Priority lowered to P3 — push capability is "nice to have" given heimdall2 doesn't currently use it.
notes: ROUND-TRIP DESIGN: when building hdf-to-asff, design the HDF<->ASFF encoding deliberately and consistently with asff-to-hdf, using our own types (NOT heimdall2's hdf2asff Types-string encoding, which was rejected/removed from asff-to-hdf). Decide: (a) does hdf-to-asff embed enough to reconstruct HDF, and if so via what mechanism; (b) does asff-to-hdf get a round-trip detection path for OUR exporter's output (analogous to CKL/CKLB's tested CKL->HDF->CKLB round-trip); (c) document asff round-trip fidelity like site/docs/guides/vex-interop.md does for VEX. Repo has no blanket round-trip guarantee - it's per-format, documented, with intentional asymmetries.

title: [chore] hdf-parsers Go: dedupe TrimSpace + string conversion in ParseResults/ParseBaseline
description:
Current PR #83 code does two `[]byte → string` conversions and two `strings.TrimSpace` passes per call:

```go
if len(strings.TrimSpace(string(input))) == 0 { … }   // alloc + trim #1 (just for len check)
input = normalizeTimestamps(input)
trimmed := strings.TrimSpace(string(input))            // alloc + trim #2 (for decoder)
```

Reorder so normalizeTimestamps runs first, then a single TrimSpace covers both purposes:

```go
input = normalizeTimestamps(input)
trimmed := strings.TrimSpace(string(input))
if len(trimmed) == 0 { return …"Input is empty" }
```

Apply to both `ParseResults` and `ParseBaseline`. Existing tests should pass unchanged; if the empty-input case currently relies on shortcutting BEFORE normalizeTimestamps, the test still passes because the regex pass over empty input is a no-op.

Probably unmeasurable on real input sizes — file it for code cleanliness, not perf.

Source: Gemini double-agent review of PR #83.
close_reason: Already shipped in PR #90 (commit 3be5e29). Closed retroactively during session-prep.

title: Add a CI gate that docs reference only real CLI commands
description:
Issue-80 doc audit found multiple speculative CLI commands documented in architecture docs that were never implemented:

- hdf system discover --aws|--k8s (described as auto-discovery, not implemented)
- hdf plan run (described as in-CLI plan execution, not implemented)
- hdf system export / hdf amend export (described as OSCAL exporters, not implemented)
- hdf evidence validate (referenced in walkthroughs; actual subcommand is verify)

These were caught manually during issue-80 cleanup. To prevent recurrence, add a CI gate that parses each doc under docs/ for hdf command references (`hdf <cmd>` in markdown code fences) and asserts each maps to a real subcommand registered via cobra. Out-of-scope commands should be tagged explicitly (e.g. inside a 'Planned' callout) and skipped.

Acceptance:
- Test or script walks docs/, extracts every `hdf <subcommand>` token, and verifies it exists in the cobra command tree.
- Commands declared as 'Planned but not yet implemented' (an explicit marker in the doc) are skipped.
- Fails CI if a docs reference doesn't resolve to a real command.

Discovered-from: issue-80 docs/architecture/ accuracy audit.

title: v3.3 CHANGELOG: clean-scan placeholder is a quiet output behavior change
description:
Issue-80 fix introduces a synthesized 'passed' placeholder for clean scans (zero findings) across 24 converters. This is correct behavior per the HDF schema, but it's a quiet behavior change for downstream consumers:

- Consumers that count total controls/requirements per baseline will see +1 (the synthesized placeholder) for clean scans where they previously saw 0.
- Consumers that group/aggregate by status will see one extra 'passed' record per clean baseline.
- The codeDesc text ('<Tool> scanned <target> and reported zero findings.') becomes visible in display layers.

Acceptance:
- CHANGELOG.md entry for v3.3.0 under 'Changed' or similar that calls out this behavior change.
- Suggested wording covers: which converters affected, why the synth was needed (schema invariant), and what downstream consumers should expect to see.
- Cross-link to docs/specification/hdf-specification.md 'Clean-scan convention' section.

title: Guard CKL/CKLB inner-empty case (iSTIG.VULN: [] / stig.rules: [])
description:
Wave 4 regression tests in issue-80 PR pinned the all-passing-rule path for ckl-to-hdf and cklb-to-hdf, but both agents independently flagged a theoretical edge case that's still unguarded:

- CKL: ParseCKL rejects input lacking <iSTIG> blocks (returns error). But an iSTIG with zero <VULN> children produces requirements: [], violating HDF schema requirements.minItems=1.
- CKLB: ParseCKLB rejects input lacking stigs[] (returns error). But a stig entry with rules: [] produces the same violation.

Unreachable via the STIG Viewer GUI that produces these files in practice — every STIG bundles N>=1 rules and STIG Viewer doesn't let users strip them. But hand-crafted JSON/XML, fuzz testing, or a malicious file could exercise this path.

Two fix options (pick whichever matches project preference):
1. Reject as malformed at parse time (extend ParseCKL/ParseCKLB to also reject empty inner arrays).
2. Synthesize a per-empty-stig placeholder using shared.BuildNoFindingsRequirement (matches the wave-1/2/3 convention).

Acceptance:
- Hand-crafted iSTIG.VULN: [] CKL is either rejected with a clear error OR converted to a baseline with one synthesized placeholder.
- Same for CKLB stig.rules: [].
- Tests pin the chosen behavior.

Discovered-from: ckl/cklb regression tests in issue-80 PR (commit 9e96fd8).
close_reason: Reject CKL iSTIG-with-no-VULN and CKLB stig-with-empty-rules at parse time (Go+TS), with tests; merged to main (a813230)

title: Analyze: should HDF schema explicitly forbid empty results[] / requirements[] arrays at converter contract level?
description:
Issue #80's suggested follow-up: 'Consider a shared schema-level invariant for the empty-array class (Bugs 2 & 3): no converter should emit requirements: [] or results: [].'

Status today: the schema already enforces Results.minItems=1 and Requirements.minItems=1 via JSON Schema. The issue isn't schema absence — it's converter compliance. So the question is really: do we need a *converter-side* shared utility / lint that asserts this invariant before output is written, beyond schema validation as a CI gate?

Investigate:
1. How many other converters silently risk this (e.g., any with conditional baseline/requirement emission paths)?
2. Would a hdf-converters/shared assertion helper (panic/throw on empty results before serialization) catch this earlier than schema validation?
3. Is this best handled by the CI round-trip gate alone (hdf-libs-ufz8) or by adding a per-emission invariant check?
4. Cost/benefit vs. ufz8 catching the same class for free.

Output: decision + recommendation. If 'yes, add a helper', file an implementation bead. If 'no, ufz8 is sufficient', close with reasoning.

Likely outcome: ufz8 suffices, but worth the half-hour to confirm.
notes:
[2026-06-03] ANALYSIS COMPLETE

## Decision

NO to a converter-side per-emission empty-array invariant helper.
YES to a different shape: CLI-layer post-conversion auto-validation. Filed as follow-up.

## Findings

1. Schema already enforces Results.minItems=1 and Requirements.minItems=1. The bugs are converter compliance gaps, not schema absence.

2. BuildHDFResults (shared/go/converterutil.go:355) takes pre-built []EvaluatedBaseline. It does NOT construct requirements/results. Adding invariant checks here would only catch issues if the caller threads in the right input — i.e., the helper is positioned downstream of where the bug actually happens.

3. Adoption surface: BuildHDFResults is used by 28/30 HDF-output converters (per existing memory). 2 bypass it (legacyhdf-to-hdf mutates post-construction). Adding a runtime check inside BuildHDFResults would not catch bypassed cases — they need the same coverage by some other route. Net: helper covers 28/30 at best.

4. Sweep result on current branch (with tlp0 fix applied):
   - INVALID against bundled fixtures: nessus-to-hdf (Bug 1), msft-defender-devops (Bug 3) — both fixture-reachable, both ufz8-catchable
   - CONV-FAIL: cyclonedx (expected per issue), scoutsuite (Bug 4 — auto-detect)
   - OK: 32 converters including aws-config-to-hdf (Bug 2 fixed)
   So today's empty-array universe is small: 1 converter against fixtures (defender-devops). Bug 2 was only reproducible against live AWS input — the bundled fixture would have shipped clean even with a per-emission helper.

5. Key surprise: hdf-cli already imports hdf-validators (ValidateResults / ValidateBaseline) — used by amend, diff, generate inspec-profile, generate upgrade — but NOT by convert.go or fetch commands. The validator is a single function call away from being invoked on every converted/fetched output.

## Why CLI-level auto-validate beats a per-emission helper

| Layer                          | Catches Bug 1+3 (fixture) | Catches Bug 2 (live)        | Cost                   | Bypass risk          |
|--------------------------------|---------------------------|------------------------------|------------------------|----------------------|
| Schema (today)                 | only if someone validates | only if someone validates    | $0                    | total                |
| ufz8 (CI gate)                 | yes                       | no (needs live or synth)     | low (one CI step)      | none for fixtures    |
| Per-emission helper (proposed) | yes (28/30 converters)    | only if test exercises empty | medium (per-converter) | legacyhdf et al.     |
| CLI post-convert validate      | yes                       | YES — first live fetch fails | low (1 fn call/site)   | --no-validate opt-out |

The CLI layer is the natural choke point. Every converted/fetched output flows through hdf convert / hdf fetch. A pre-write ValidateResults call catches anything the schema rejects — including future invariants we havent thought of yet, and including live-input bugs that fixtures cannot cover.

## What ufz8 still buys us

CI fail-fast for PR review, decoupled from any user invoking the CLI. Worth keeping as a belt-and-suspenders.

## Recommendation

1. Close 8vbp with this analysis.
2. File follow-up bead: hdf convert / hdf fetch auto-validate output before writing (--no-validate opt-out). Targets the empty-array class AND the next class of schema-violation bugs we havent surfaced yet.
3. Do NOT migrate converters to use a shared empty-check helper — low ROI, high surface area.

## Out-of-scope but worth noting

The CLI auto-validate idea may want to expand to hdf-to-* converters (CKL, CSV, OSCAL, XCCDF, XML) that have their own format-specific schemas. Out of scope for this bead but mention in the follow-up.
close_reason: Analysis complete. Decision: NO converter-side per-emission helper (low ROI vs. schema + CI gate + migration cost). Proposed and filed sedq instead — CLI-layer auto-validate is a smaller, more centralized change that catches both fixture-reachable and live-input bug classes.

title: amend apply: one amendments file to many results files
description:
## General amend improvement (all override types, not CVE-specific)

Today `hdf amend apply` takes a single --results and a single --amendments (both required, single-valued). An amendment is reusable org context that should apply across many results files (different scans, different systems, over time). Support that directly instead of forcing N separate invocations.

## Desired shape (aligns with SAF CLI attest apply)

SAF's `attest apply -i <files>...` accepts multiple HDF + attestation files, sniffs each by shape, and writes to a directory when multiple executions are present. Mirror that:
- Accept multiple results files (and/or a glob/dir).
- One amendments file applied to each.
- Output: single file when one result, a directory when many.

## Notes

- Expiry is anchored at the amendment's appliedAt (absolute) — applying the SAME amendment to results collected at different times still expires on the same absolute date. Do NOT restart any clock per-apply (see hdf-libs-z0z7).
- Keep the existing single --results/--amendments form working (back-compat).
- Per-result chain integrity (previousChecksum) still computed per output.

## Surfaced during

hdf-libs-j3s6 design discussion. Was assumed to already work — it does not; also a test gap (no coverage because the feature is absent).

title: amend: accept relative duration (1y/6m/2w) for expiresAt, resolve to absolute at create
description:
## QOL — general amend improvement (all override types, not CVE-specific)

Let amend authors enter a relative TTL (e.g. 1y, 6m, 2w, 90d) instead of spelling out an absolute ISO date for expiresAt. Resolve to an absolute timestamp ONCE, at create time: expiresAt = appliedAt + duration. Storage stays absolute; apply never recomputes it.

## Why absolute storage (NOT relative semantics)

An amendment (attestation/waiver/etc.) is a point-in-time assessment with a fixed TTL from when the assessment/interview happened. The clock must NOT restart each time the amendment is applied to a new results file — Heimdall2 flipped an attested requirement back to notReviewed once the ORIGINAL absolute expiry passed. We are only stealing SAF CLI's input ergonomic (type "1y"), not relative expiration semantics. SAF itself should arguably not be doing relative-at-apply either.

## Scope

- Duration parser: N[d|w|m|y] (+ maybe fractional like 1.5y). Applies to interactive create, headless create, and amend set.
- expiresAt input accepts EITHER an absolute ISO date OR a duration; duration resolves against appliedAt (or now) at write time.
- Applies to ALL override types — attestation, waiver, poam, riskAdjustment, falsePositive, etc.

## Surfaced during

hdf-libs-j3s6 (CVSS enrichment) design discussion, but this is a general amend QOL improvement.
close_reason: Shipped: parseExpiryInput (amend_create.go:446-469) and normalizeExpiresAt (amend_headless.go:262) parse Nd/Nm/Ny against an anchor; tests pin 1y and 6m resolution (amend_headless_test.go:119,299,383,621,664). Closed via board audit 2026-06-15.

title: Investigate bundling a CVSS calculator into hdf-libs
description:
## Background

During epic hdf-libs-8zn0 we explicitly deferred a CVSS scoring engine — hdf-utilities ships parseCvssVector + validateCvssVector (syntactic only), and we pointed consumers at pandatix/go-cvss (Go) and the npm cvss package for actual score computation. Storing structured inputs was the value-add; recomputation was treated as a consumer concern.

Revisiting that decision — there is real pull for an in-house calculator. This bead is an INVESTIGATION, not a commitment to build.

## Why reconsider

- effectiveCvss (hdf-libs-ib3o) needs to recompute a final score after applying consumer Environmental/Threat metrics. Without a bundled calculator, that resolution either depends on an external lib or cannot be done in-process.
- The consumer-enrichment workflow (hdf-libs-ib3o) wants to validate that a consumer-supplied impact.value is consistent with the recomputed cvss.computedScore — currently a soft documented rule, not enforced, because we have no calculator.
- Dual TS + Go parity: any external dependency must exist + behave identically in both languages, which is exactly the kind of drift hdf-utilities exists to prevent.

## Investigation questions

1. Scope: which CVSS versions must we compute? v3.1 + v4.0 at minimum; v2.0 + v3.0 for legacy ingestion. Each has a distinct formula.
2. Build vs depend vs vendor:
   - Build: ~200-400 LOC per version per language, but full control + TS/Go parity guaranteed. FIRST publishes reference formulas + test vectors.
   - Depend: pandatix/go-cvss (Go, mature) + npm cvss or @pandatix/josiah — but parity across two ecosystems is the risk, and npm CVSS libs vary in v4 support.
   - Vendor: copy + adapt a permissively-licensed implementation into hdf-utilities.
3. Where it lives: hdf-utilities/{src,go}/cvss/ alongside the existing parser, exporting computeCvssScore(vector) -> {score, severity}.
4. Test strategy: FIRST publishes official test vectors per version — validate against those, not hand-rolled cases. This is the one place we can use authoritative reference data instead of converter fixtures.
5. v4.0 specifically: the v4 scoring algorithm is substantially more complex than v3 (MacroVector lookup table + interpolation). Confirm a correct, license-compatible reference exists before committing.

## Acceptance (for the investigation)

- A short recommendation doc: build vs depend vs vendor, with the v4.0 complexity assessment as the deciding factor.
- If "build": a follow-up implementation bead with scoped LOC estimate.
- Confirm FIRST test-vector availability for TDD.

## Dependencies

- Unblocks the score-recomputation parts of hdf-libs-ib3o (effectiveCvss + enrichment consistency check).

## Parent epic

hdf-libs-8zn0

Specifically exercise applicability against the conventions the RFC
flagged as today's wild west:

title: Populate v3.2 classification fields in existing converters

Easy wins:
  - XCCDF -> HDF: controlType heuristic from family prefix
    (PM-* / *-1 -> management; AT-* / IR-* / MA-* -> operational;
    AC-3 / SC-* / SI-* / etc. -> technical). Skip for IDs that don't
    match a family (e.g. SV-* STIG IDs without a NIST tag).
  - Any converter where check code is non-null can set
    verificationMethod=automated; null code with explicit policy
    indicators -> manual-by-design.
  - applicability defaults to omitted (= 'required'); only set when
    the source format encodes it explicitly.

Each converter is its own small change. Don't try to populate everywhere
at once — pick the high-value ones (XCCDF, OSCAL, CIS) and leave the
rest as omitted.

Out of scope:
  - Hand-curating controlType for every NIST 800-53 control (separate
    content effort, sourced from SP 800-53A assessment-objects)

title: hdf-parsers: improve mutation test coverage (36 survived, 38 no-cov)
description:
Stryker mutation testing scored hdf-parsers at **50.00%** (36 survived, 38 no-coverage) when run on unit tests only. Integration tests were excluded because Stryker's sandbox doesn't include sibling-package fixture files. Stryker config is at `hdf-parsers/stryker.config.cjs`.
